meta.ogDescription: Verified: Abraham Maslow wrote this exact sentence in The Psychology of Science (1966), pp. 15–16. The idea, though, was Abraham Kaplan's first.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This one is real, word for word. Maslow wrote the sentence in The Psychology of Science: A Reconnaissance (Harper & Row, New York, 1966); Quote Investigator ↗ verified it on paper at pages 15–16, and Wikiquote ↗ cites it to chapter 2, page 15. What is not purely his is the thought behind it — the philosopher Abraham Kaplan was circulating a boy-with-a-hammer version years earlier.

source.excerpt: I remember seeing an elaborate and complicated automatic washing machine for automobiles that did a beautiful job of washing them. … I suppose it is tempting, if the only tool you have is a hammer, to treat everything as if it were a nail.
trail: The anchor. Quote Investigator ↗ cites the sentence to “The Psychology of Science: A Reconnaissance by Abraham H. Maslow, Quote Page 15 and 16, Published by Harper & Row, New York,” and marks the citation “Verified on paper.”

Second, independent confirmation. Wikiquote ↗ carries the line in its main sourced 1960s section — the page has no Disputed or Misattributed section at all — citing The Psychology of Science: A Reconnaissance (1966), ch. 2, p. 15.

The edition checks out. The Internet Archive catalogue record ↗ confirms the first edition: Harper & Row, New York, 1966, LCCN 66011479. The scan is access-restricted, so the page image is not publicly readable.

The one caveat. The idea is older than the sentence. Quote Investigator’s chronology places Abraham Kaplan’s boy-with-a-hammer version in February 1962 and in The Conduct of Inquiry (1964), and Wikipedia’s law of the instrument ↗ article notes the concept is credited to both men.
source.excerptNote: Two sentences from the same passage. The hammer sentence is the one Quote Investigator ↗ verified on paper at pages 15 and 16; the car-wash sentence that sets it up is transcribed in Wikipedia’s law of the instrument ↗ article. The ellipsis marks material between them that we have not seen in the original and so do not reproduce.

author.name: Abraham Maslow
author.heading: Who was Abraham Maslow?
author.bio: Abraham Harold Maslow (1 April 1908 – 8 June 1970) was an American psychologist best known for Maslow’s hierarchy of needs, his theory of psychological health built on fulfilling innate human needs in priority order, culminating in self-actualization. He taught at Brooklyn College and Brandeis University, and was a founding figure of humanistic psychology. In 1966 he published The Psychology of Science: A Reconnaissance, a critique of how method-bound researchers narrow the questions they are willing to ask — the book that contains this sentence.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong about it
misattribution.intro: The sentence itself is sound — this is one of the rare famous-psychologist quotes that survives checking. The trouble is everything that has grown around it: a shortened pop version that is not Maslow’s wording, and a concept named after him that somebody else stated first.

items.why: The concept now called “Maslow’s hammer” was in circulation before Maslow’s book. Quote Investigator ↗ documents the UCLA philosopher Abraham Kaplan telling an American Educational Research Association banquet in February 1962 that “Give a boy a hammer and everything he meets has to be pounded,” and printing “Give a small boy a hammer, and he will find that everything he encounters needs pounding” on page 28 of The Conduct of Inquiry (Chandler, 1964). Wikipedia’s law of the instrument ↗ article calls Kaplan’s 1964 formulation the first recorded statement of the concept.

items.who: Nobody in particular — a later compression
items.why: “If all you have is a hammer, everything looks like a nail” is not what Maslow wrote. Wikipedia describes it explicitly as the way Maslow’s hammer is popularly phrased ↗, not as his sentence. Maslow’s own line is longer, hedged and much more tentative: it begins “I suppose it is tempting…”

The tightest version in circulation — “to a man with a hammer, everything looks like a nail” — is frequently quoted as though it were Maslow’s own words. It is not; Quote Investigator’s timeline ↗ records Warren Buffett using that phrasing in the journal Hermes in 1984.

The image is far older than any of them. Quote Investigator ↗ traces it back to an anonymous piece called “Toys” in the periodical Once a Week in 1868: “Give a boy a hammer and chisel; show him how to use them; at once he begins to hack the doorposts…”

misattribution.truthLine: The verdict: the sentence is genuinely Maslow’s, printed in The Psychology of Science in 1966 and verified on paper ↗ at pages 15–16. Quote it as his — but quote it in full, and know that Abraham Kaplan got there first with the thought.

context.heading: Why the sentence landed
lead: Maslow was not writing about carpentry. The Psychology of Science is an argument about researchers who let their favourite method decide which problems are worth having. The passage that carries this line opens with a machine: “I remember seeing an elaborate and complicated automatic washing machine for automobiles that did a beautiful job of washing them” — a device that was superb at exactly one thing and useless at everything else, as transcribed in Wikipedia’s law of the instrument ↗ article.

The idea now travels under the name Maslow’s hammer, which is a little unfair to Abraham Kaplan. Wikipedia calls Kaplan’s 1964 formulation “the first recorded statement of the concept,” while Quote Investigator ↗ documents Kaplan saying a version of it at an American Educational Research Association banquet in February 1962. Maslow’s contribution was the phrasing — he was the one who reached for the word nail in the shape everybody now repeats.
detailsBody: 1868 — an anonymous piece titled “Toys” in the periodical Once a Week: “Give a boy a hammer and chisel; show him how to use them; at once he begins to hack the doorposts…”
February 1962 — Abraham Kaplan, in a banquet speech to the American Educational Research Association: “Give a boy a hammer and everything he meets has to be pounded.” No nail.
1963 — Silvan Tomkins, in Computer Simulation of Personality: “If one has a hammer one tends to look for nails” — the first appearance of the nail in Quote Investigator’s timeline.
1964 — Abraham Kaplan, The Conduct of Inquiry: Methodology for Behavioral Science, page 28: “Give a small boy a hammer, and he will find that everything he encounters needs pounding.”
1966 — Abraham Maslow, The Psychology of Science, pages 15–16: the sentence on this page.
1984 — Warren Buffett, in the journal Hermes: “to a man with a hammer, everything looks like a nail” — the compressed form that now often gets pinned back onto Maslow.
context.pull: Kaplan had the idea. Maslow had the sentence.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator cites the exact wording to Abraham Maslow, The Psychology of Science: A Reconnaissance, Harper & Row, New York, pages 15 and 16, marked 'Verified on paper'.
Quote Investigator documents Abraham Kaplan saying 'Give a boy a hammer and everything he meets has to be pounded' at an American Educational Research Association banquet speech in February 1962.

Quote Investigator cites Abraham Kaplan, The Conduct of Inquiry: Methodology for Behavioral Science, page 28, Chandler Publishing Company, San Francisco (1964): 'Give a small boy a hammer, and he will find that everything he encounters needs pounding.'
Quote Investigator's chronology includes an 1868 item titled 'Toys' in the periodical Once a Week: 'Give a boy a hammer and chisel; show him how to use them; at once he begins to hack the doorposts…'
Quote Investigator's chronology includes Silvan Tomkins in Computer Simulation of Personality (1963): 'If one has a hammer one tends to look for nails.'
Quote Investigator's chronology records Warren Buffett using 'to a man with a hammer, everything looks like a nail' in the journal Hermes in 1984.

Quote Investigator concludes that Kaplan formulated a version by 1962 without the word 'nail', Tomkins used 'nail' in 1963 in a differing form, and Maslow's 1966 version is the one similar to popular expressions circulating today.

Wikiquote lists the quote in its main sourced 1960s section (not Disputed or Misattributed), cited to The Psychology of Science: A Reconnaissance (1966), ch. 2, p. 15; the page has no Misattributed or Disputed section.

Wikipedia's 'Law of the instrument' article names the concept 'Maslow's hammer', gives the popular phrasing 'if all you have is a hammer, everything looks like a nail', transcribes Maslow's automatic car-washing machine sentence, states that Kaplan's 1964 formulation was 'the first recorded statement of the concept', and notes the concept is attributed to both Maslow and Kaplan.

Wikipedia gives Abraham Maslow's dates as 1 April 1908 – 8 June 1970, describes him as an American psychologist known for the hierarchy of needs who taught at Brooklyn College and Brandeis University, notes his 1966 publication of The Psychology of Science: A Reconnaissance, and mentions 'Maslow's hammer'.

The Internet Archive record for psychologyofscie00masl is Abraham H. Maslow, 'The psychology of science; a reconnaissance', publisher Harper & Row, New York, 1966, LCCN 66011479, and the item is access-restricted (not freely readable).
